stat_summary: Red-green colour vision deficiency, the most common form of colour blindness, occurs in about 1 in 12 men and 1 in 200 women among people of Northern European ancestry, according to NIH MedlinePlus Genetics. The condition is inherited in an X-linked pattern, which is why it is much more frequent in men.
stat_source_title: Color vision deficiency, NIH MedlinePlus Genetics

male.headline: It's Not a Joke: One in 12 Men Can't Tell Red from Green, and the World Was Not Designed With Them in Mind
male.standfirst: Official medical figures confirm what every bloke already knows from a packet of wires and a badly printed map: a common, everyday disadvantage is still treated as a punchline, and men are the ones living with it.
male.image_caption: Pete, 42, fairly sure one of these is the live one.
body_paragraphs: Official medical figures have confirmed what every bloke already knows from a packet of wires and a badly printed map: red-green colour blindness is not a rare curiosity. Among people of Northern European ancestry it affects about 1 in 12 men – and about 1 in 200 women – and the world of traffic lights, charts, school worksheets and barbecue instructions has not been designed with them in mind.
“I held up two reels of cable in the garage and still couldn't swear which was live,” said Pete, 42, from Portsmouth. “Everybody thought it was hilarious. Nobody offered to label the fuse box.”

Researchers note that the condition is X-linked, which is why it lands so much more often on men, and that it usually leaves sharpness of vision intact, which is why it is so easy to dismiss. Campaigners are already calling for a National Ishihara Day, and for every public map, pie chart and 'cook until golden brown' instruction to come with, in their words, “a version a bloke can actually use”.
Yet where is the outrage? Where is the documentary? Britain's unacknowledged one-in-twelve squints on, alone, with only a 50-50 guess for company.
male.pull_quote: Everybody thought it was hilarious. Nobody offered to label the fuse box.

female.headline: The Unofficial Colour Department: Women Spend Their Lives Answering 'Does This Match?', and It's No Coincidence
female.standfirst: The same figures that show colour blindness is rare in women also explain a familiar household job: when 1 in 12 men cannot tell the difference, someone has to.
body_paragraphs: The same official figures that show red-green colour blindness is rare in women – about 1 in 200, against 1 in 12 men – also explain a job that never appears on any timesheet. When so many of the men in a woman's life cannot reliably tell the shades apart, she becomes the household's unofficial colour department.

“He asked me whether the shirt went with the jumper, then whether the burger was cooked, then which wire was which,” said Linda, 46, from York. “I have been head of quality control since 2009, and nobody's put it on the mortgage.”

Because the condition is so much more common in men, the knock-on labour – matching school jumpers, reading the chart, confirming that the traffic light really is the one he thinks it is – falls, day after day, to women. Campaigners are demanding a Colour Consultancy Allowance and a national apology for the phrase “you choose, you're better at this”.
Until then, the country's unpaid shade-matchers will keep holding things up to the window, one almost-identical jumper at a time.
female.pull_quote: I have been head of quality control since 2009, and nobody's put it on the mortgage.
